helpful clue to an accurate diagnosis. Further complicating the diagnosis is the genetic diversity of the disease, in that X-linked, autosomal recessive, and autosomal dominant forms of the disease exist. $^{9}$

This means that dyskeratosis congenita (DC) can be passed down through families in different patterns—sometimes linked to the X chromosome (affecting mostly males), sometimes requiring two copies of a faulty gene (one from each parent), and sometimes only one copy being enough to cause disease. This genetic variety makes family history interpretation more complex and underscores why genetic testing must be broad and thoughtful.
The implicated genes are involved in telomere maintenance, resulting in shortened telomeres in patients with DC mutations. $^{10,11}$

Let’s unpack that. Telomeres are like the protective plastic tips on the ends of shoelaces—but for chromosomes. Every time a cell divides, these telomeres get a little shorter. Normally, certain proteins help rebuild them, keeping cells healthy and able to divide over time. In DC, the genes responsible for maintaining telomeres are broken, so the telomeres shorten too quickly. This leads to premature aging of cells, especially in tissues that divide frequently—like bone marrow, skin, and the lining of the mouth. That’s why patients often show signs like abnormal skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia, along with bone marrow failure.

Although several of these genes are available for clinical testing, a negative test result does not eliminate DC from the differential because the pathologic genetic mutations are uncharacteristic in approximately 50% of DC cases. $^{11}$

In other words, even if we test the known DC-related genes and find nothing, we still can’t rule out the disease. Why? Because there may be other, as-yet-undiscovered genes involved, or mutations in non-coding regions that standard tests don’t catch. This is a great example of how medicine often deals with probabilities rather than certainties—especially in rare diseases. So, clinicians must rely not just on genetics, but also on clinical features and telomere length testing (which can show abnormally short telomeres, supporting the diagnosis even without a known mutation).

Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is another rare cause of pancytopenia, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, and usually presenting in infancy with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and bone marrow failure. Most cases are associated with mutations in chromosome 7 affecting the Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome (SBDS) gene. $^{12,13}$

Let’s break this down: “Autosomal recessive” means a child must inherit two faulty copies of the gene—one from each parent—to develop the disease. The SBDS gene plays a role in ribosome assembly, which is essential for protein production in cells. When this process is disrupted, rapidly dividing cells—like those in the bone marrow and pancreas—are hit hardest.

Neutropenia is the most common presentation of this bone marrow failure, and the marrow cellularity can be low, normal, or high, and mildly dysplastic features can be seen. The condition progresses to complete bone marrow failure in $20\%$ to $25\%$ of patients and to MDS/AML in $5\%$ to $33\%$ of patients. $^{14}$

So, while low neutrophil counts are typical, the bone marrow doesn’t always look empty—sometimes it’s normal or even crowded, which can be confusing. The presence of mild dysplasia (abnormal-looking cells) might raise suspicion for myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), but in Shwachman-Diamond, it’s part of the baseline picture. The risk of progression to full marrow failure or leukemia is real, which is why ongoing monitoring is crucial.

Again, bone marrow findings are nonspecific but should be evaluated to eliminate other causes of bone marrow failure. Cytogenetic abnormalities of chromosome 7 can be helpful clues to a diagnosis of Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and genetic testing can also be helpful, but $10\%$ of patients will not carry a mutation in the SBDS gene.

This is another reminder that negative genetic testing doesn’t rule out the disease—some patients have mutations in other genes or in regulatory regions not covered by standard assays. So, a clinical diagnosis—based on symptoms, lab findings, and imaging—remains essential.
In addition, other causes of pancreatic insufficiency should be entertained, with sweat chloride test results being normal in this disease, compared with cystic fibrosis.

That’s a key point. Babies with Shwachman-Diamond can have fatty stools and poor growth due to pancreatic enzyme deficiency—just like in cystic fibrosis. But unlike CF, their sweat chloride test (a standard diagnostic test for CF) is normal. This distinction is critical to avoid misdiagnosis and ensure proper management.

Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (CAMT) is an additional cause of congenital bone marrow failure and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, often because of mutations in myeloproliferative leukemia virus oncogene (MPL, or the thrombopoietin receptor). $^{15,16}$

MPL is the receptor for thrombopoietin (TPO), the main hormone that tells the bone marrow to make platelets. If the receptor is broken, the signal doesn’t get through—even if TPO levels are high. It’s like having a ringing phone with a dead battery: the call is coming in, but no one can answer.
Patients usually are seen as neonates with severe thrombocytopenia and its clinical sequelae, including petechiae, purpura, or bleeding of the skin, mucous membranes, and/or gastrointestinal tract.
So right from birth, these babies are at high risk for bleeding because they can’t make enough platelets. The absence of megakaryocytes—the platelet-producing cells—in the bone marrow is a hallmark.

In approximately 25% of patients, the condition progresses to pancytopenia, usually between 3 and 4 years of age. On peripheral smear, platelets remain normal in size, and bone marrow biopsy, although initially normocellular and demonstrating reduced or absent megakaryocytes, can evolve quite early and quickly to aplasia. $^{17}$

This progression is insidious: the marrow starts out looking relatively normal in cellularity (not empty), but over time, all blood cell lines fail. That’s why early diagnosis and planning for hematopoietic stem cell transplant—the only cure—are so important.

In its pancytopenic presentation, the differential diagnosis includes other bone marrow failure syndromes, and a complete workup, including chromosomal breakage studies, should be performed to eliminate such entities as FA. Genetic analysis for mutations in MPL can additionally be performed, but a negative result does not preclude the diagnosis of CAMT.
Again, we see the theme: genetic testing is helpful, but not definitive. Some patients may have mutations in regulatory regions or other genes not routinely tested.
Finally, patients with CAMT often have high circulating levels of thrombopoietin, which can also be tested. $^{18}$

This makes perfect sense: if the bone marrow can’t respond to TPO, the body keeps producing more in a futile attempt to stimulate platelet production. So, elevated TPO levels in a baby with thrombocytopenia and no MPL mutation? That’s a strong clue pointing toward CAMT.

Another rare and complex syndrome that can present with pancytopenia is hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), which can be either primary or acquired. The clinical diagnosis of this syndrome requires the presence of 5 or more of the following: fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia involving 2 or more cell lines, hypertriglyceridemia or hypofibrinogenemia, hepatitis, low or absent natural killer cell activity, a serum ferritin level higher than 500
soluble CD25 higher than 2,400 U/mL, or hemophagocytosis as demonstrated in bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node. $^{19}$

of HLH as a “cytokine storm” of the immune system. It’s not a cancer, but an overreaction—like a fire alarm that won’t turn off. Immune cells (especially T cells and macrophages) become hyperactivated and start attacking the body’s own tissues, including blood cells and organs. This leads to fever, organ enlargement, low blood counts, and metabolic chaos. The diagnostic criteria are designed to capture this systemic inflammation.

First described in 1952, the primary familial form of this disorder occurs most often in infants younger than 1 year, and has been found to be the result of uncontrolled T-cell and histiocyte activation. $^{20}$

In healthy people, cytotoxic T cells kill infected or abnormal cells and then shut down. In primary HLH, genetic defects prevent this shutdown. It’s like having a car with no brakes—the immune system accelerates but can’t stop.
Mutations in several proteins, including perforin 1, UNC13D, and syntaxin 11, have been implicated in this disease. $^{21-23}$

These proteins are essential for cytotoxic granules to release their contents into target cells. If any part of this machinery is broken, dead cells aren’t cleared properly, and the immune system keeps getting activated. It’s a vicious cycle.
Interestingly, the syndrome is most often triggered by a stimulus, such as infection, and numerous viruses, bacteria, and parasites have been implicated. $^{24}$
So even in genetic forms, a “second hit”—like a viral infection—often sets off the cascade. This is why HLH can appear suddenly after a seemingly routine illness.
Primary HLH can also occur in patients with immune deficiencies, including Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, Griscelli syndrome 2, and X-linked lymphoproliferative disease.
These are all conditions where the immune system’s ability to kill infected cells is impaired—making HLH a common and dangerous complication.

Because HLH is rapidly fatal, a high diagnostic suspicion should be entertained. Bone marrow biopsy can be helpful, and the finding of hemophagocytosis in the bone marrow, spleen, or lymph nodes is indeed one of the diagnostic criteria for HLH, as mentioned before.
Hemophagocytosis means macrophages are actively engulfing red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets—literally “eating” the blood. It’s a dramatic sign of immune system overactivation.

However, the sensitivity of bone marrow morphologic analysis for hemophagocytosis is surprisingly low; however, hemophagocytosis may be more easily identified on iron-stained marrow aspirate smears than typical Wright-stained smears. In a postmortem study, hemophagocytosis was seen in the bone marrow of only 9 of 23 children with HLH and was more commonly seen in sections of the spleen (17/24 patients) and lymph nodes (17/23 patients). $^{25}$

This is a critical point: a normal bone marrow biopsy does not rule out HLH. The absence of hemophagocytosis doesn’t mean the disease isn’t there—it might just be missed, or the process might be happening elsewhere.
Similarly, a Canadian study determined a sensitivity of only 60% in finding hemophagocytosis in the initial bone marrow biopsy of patients with HLH. $^{26}$

In addition to congenital causes of bone marrow failure, numerous acquired causes of bone marrow failure exist. Indeed, AA is relatively common, and is seen in both children and adults. Although the majority of cases are idiopathic, this disease can be caused by multiple etiologies, including drugs, chemicals, radiation, viruses, anorexia, and even pregnancy. Patients often present with an abrupt onset of pancytopenia and a remarkably reduced bone marrow cellularity.

Think of hematopoietic stem cells as the factory workers in a bustling blood cell factory (the bone marrow). If these workers are wiped out, the factory shuts down. This leads to **bone marrow failure**, where the marrow becomes empty or "hypocellular," and **peripheral pancytopenia**, meaning dangerously low levels of all blood cell types in the bloodstream. This explains the common symptoms of AA: fatigue (from anemia), infections (from low white cells), and bleeding (from low platelets).

Now, here’s a key clue that supports the autoimmune theory: **AA often responds remarkably well to immunosuppressive therapy**—drugs that dampen the immune system, essentially telling the rogue T cells to stand down. This response is like catching the immune system red-handed. If suppressing the immune system helps the bone marrow recover, it strongly suggests the immune system was the attacker all along. Long-term survival with treatment is estimated at approximately 75%, a testament to the effectiveness of these therapies when appropriately applied.

So how do we define *severe* aplastic anemia? It’s not enough to just suspect AA—we need clear, measurable criteria. These are outlined in **Table 2**, and a diagnosis of severe AA requires meeting at least two of the following blood findings:

- **Reticulocytes <1%**, corrected for hematocrit: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells. A low count means the bone marrow isn’t producing new red cells. The correction for hematocrit adjusts for the patient’s current red cell volume, making the measurement more accurate.
- **Absolute neutrophil count < 500/μL (0.5 × 10⁹/L)**: Neutrophils are critical infection-fighting white blood cells. This extremely low level puts patients at high risk for life-threatening infections.
- **Platelets < 20,000/μL (20 × 10⁹/L)**: Platelets are essential for clotting. At this level, spontaneous bleeding (like nosebleeds or bruising) becomes a serious concern.

In addition to these blood findings, we must also assess the bone marrow itself. Severe AA is confirmed if the bone marrow biopsy shows:

- **Less than 25% normal cellularity**, OR
- **Less than 50% normal cellularity** with **fewer than 30% hematopoietic cells** (the blood-forming cells) among the remaining cells.

This distinction is important: even if the marrow isn’t extremely empty (below 25%), if it’s less than half full and most of what’s left isn’t blood-forming tissue, it still qualifies as severe AA.

When we look at the blood in AA, we typically see **pancytopenia**—low counts across all cell lines. Interestingly, the proportion of lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) often appears increased. This isn’t because lymphocytes are multiplying; rather, it’s a *relative* increase because all the other cell types are so depleted. It’s like having only one red car in a parking lot full of blue cars—the red car stands out, not because there are more red cars, but because the blue ones are gone.

The bone marrow biopsy usually reveals a **markedly hypocellular** (very empty) marrow, with a dramatic reduction in all three blood cell lineages: red cells, white cells, and platelets. However, among the few remaining cells, we often find an increased proportion of **T lymphocytes**. This fits perfectly with the autoimmune theory—these are likely the very cells that are attacking the stem cells.

Now, here’s where things get tricky: **distinguishing severe AA from hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)** can be extremely difficult. Both conditions present with low blood counts and a low-cellularity bone marrow. But they are fundamentally different: AA is an immune-mediated destruction, while MDS is a pre-leukemic condition where blood cells are produced but are dysfunctional and prone to becoming leukemia.

So how do we tell them apart? We need to dig deeper. Careful examination of the bone marrow **aspirate smears** and **touch preparations** (direct impressions of the marrow on a slide) is crucial. We’re looking for **morphologic dysplasia**—abnormal shapes, sizes, or structures in the blood cells. Dysplasia is a hallmark of MDS, not AA.

But sometimes, the cells look normal despite low counts. That’s where **cytogenetic studies** (looking for chromosomal abnormalities) and **immunohistochemical studies** (using antibodies to detect specific proteins in cells) come in. Certain chromosomal changes are strongly linked to MDS and are rare in AA. These are listed in **Table 3**.

For example, losing part or all of chromosome 7 (written as -7 or del(7q)) or chromosome 5 (-5 or del(5q)) is a red flag for MDS. These abnormalities disrupt genes involved in normal blood cell development and are uncommon in pure AA.

Another helpful clue: **immunohistochemical staining for CD34**, a marker of immature blood cells. In hypoplastic MDS, we often see an **increase in CD34-positive cells**, indicating a buildup of abnormal immature cells. In contrast, in AA, CD34+ cells are typically **very low or absent**, reflecting the overall depletion of stem cells.

It’s also worth noting that the relationship between AA and MDS isn’t always clear-cut. **Some patients initially diagnosed with AA later develop features of MDS**. This evolution suggests that in some cases, what looks like immune destruction might actually be an early phase of a clonal disorder, or that the bone marrow damage in AA creates an environment where abnormal clones can emerge.

Adding another layer of complexity is **paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)**, a rare blood disorder with a fascinating and intricate relationship to AA.

PNH arises from a mutation in the **PIGA gene** (phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation class A). This gene is essential for making a molecular anchor called **GPI (glycosylphosphatidylinositol)** that attaches certain protective proteins to the surface of blood cells. When PIGA is defective, these proteins—like CD55 and CD59, which normally shield cells from the immune system’s complement attack—are missing. As a result, PNH cells are **extra vulnerable to complement-mediated destruction**, leading to **intravascular hemolysis**—the breaking open of red blood cells within blood vessels, especially at night (hence "nocturnal hemoglobinuria").

PNH can occur on its own (de novo), and in those cases, patients often have a **normocellular or even hypercellular bone marrow**—the opposite of AA—along with hemolysis, low blood counts, and a high risk of blood clots (venous thrombosis).

But here’s the twist: **PNH and AA are closely linked**. Many patients with AA have small populations of PNH cells detectable by sensitive flow cytometry. In fact, **up to two-thirds of patients with pancytopenic AA have small PNH clones**. Conversely, about **30% of PNH patients had signs of AA before their PNH diagnosis**.

Why does this happen? One theory is that in AA, the immune system attacks normal hematopoietic stem cells, but **PNH cells, lacking GPI-anchored proteins, are invisible to the immune attack**. So, while normal stem cells are destroyed, PNH clones survive and expand—a brutal example of "survival of the fittest" in a diseased marrow. This gives PNH cells a selective advantage.

Yet, despite how common these small PNH clones are in AA patients, **progression to full-blown, symptomatic PNH is rare**. A recent study found that only **2.1% of AA patients developed clinical PNH within 5 years**. This suggests that most PNH clones remain small and clinically silent, likely because they don’t have additional mutations needed to cause overt disease.

Although B-lymphoblastic leukemia generally presents with cytopenias (low blood counts), the peripheral blood is often involved by B lymphoblasts, and therefore the leukocyte count may be decreased, normal, or markedly elevated. This might seem counterintuitive—how can someone have low white blood cells overall but also have leukemia, which is a cancer of white blood cells? The key is understanding what kind of white blood cells we're counting. In this case, the high number (if present) comes from circulating immature, non-functional B lymphoblasts. These cells are counted in the total white blood cell (WBC) count, but they don’t work like normal white blood cells. So a patient could have a sky-high WBC count full of useless blasts and still be immunocompromised and prone to infection. Conversely, if the marrow is so packed that even blast cells can’t get into the bloodstream efficiently, the WBC count might be low. This variability underscores why you can't diagnose or rule out leukemia based on the WBC count alone.

Bone marrow examination is usually diagnostic and generally demonstrates replacement of marrow space by sheets of B lymphoblasts. Imagine looking under the microscope at a normal bone marrow sample: you'd see a diverse mix of developing red cells, white cells, and platelet precursors, all in balance. In B-lymphoblastic leukemia, that picture is replaced by a uniform sea of identical-looking immature lymphoid cells—like a field of clones. This "effacement" of normal architecture is a hallmark of acute leukemia.

Of course, flow cytometric and cytogenetic studies should be performed concomitantly with bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for proper classification. Why are these tests so important? Morphology (what the cells look like under the microscope) can suggest the diagnosis, but it can’t tell us the full story. Flow cytometry analyzes proteins on the surface of cells—like molecular ID tags. For B-lymphoblastic leukemia, we expect to see markers such as CD19, CD10, CD22, and PAX5, which identify the cells as being of B-cell lineage. This helps distinguish it from T-lymphoblastic leukemia or acute myeloid leukemia, which have different marker profiles. Cytogenetic studies look at the chromosomes inside the cells. Certain genetic abnormalities—like the Philadelphia chromosome (translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22)—have major implications for prognosis and treatment. So while the bone marrow biopsy shows *that* something is wrong, flow cytometry and cytogenetics tell us *exactly what kind* of leukemia it is and how aggressive it might be.

Prognosis is generally favorable in children, with a 10-year 63% event-free survival seen in children; however, this number drops to 25% to 35% in adults. This striking difference highlights a key principle in oncology: age is not just a number—it reflects underlying biological differences in disease behavior and treatment tolerance. Childhood B-ALL tends to have more favorable genetic profiles and children tolerate intensive chemotherapy better than adults. Adults, on the other hand, often have higher-risk genetic mutations and may not withstand the same treatment intensity, contributing to poorer outcomes.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is generally a disease of childhood, whereas AML is usually a disease of adults, accounting for 80% of the acute leukemic cases in adults. This age dichotomy is more than just an epidemiological curiosity—it reflects fundamental differences in the origins and biology of these diseases. ALL often arises from errors during early lymphoid development, which is more active in children. AML, in contrast, often stems from accumulated genetic damage over time, which aligns with aging and prior exposures (like chemotherapy or radiation), making it more common in older adults.

Currently, the World Health Organization classifies such leukemias into several categories, including AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, therapy-related myeloid
neoplasms, AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities, and AML, not otherwise specified.

This classification isn’t just academic—it directly guides treatment and predicts outcomes. For example, AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities (like t(8;21) or inv(16)) tends to respond well to chemotherapy, while therapy-related AML (arising after prior chemo or radiation) is often more resistant and aggressive. Each category tells a different story about the disease’s origin and behavior.
As with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, patients with AML often have complications of cytopenias, including weakness, fatigability, bleeding, or infection.
The root cause is the same: malignant blasts take over the bone marrow and suppress normal hematopoiesis. But here’s a critical point: blasts
may not be present on the peripheral smear, but usually can be found.

That means even if the initial blood smear doesn’t show obvious blasts, you can’t rule out AML. Sometimes the blasts are trapped in the marrow (a phenomenon called “maturation arrest” or “myelophthisis”), or they’re present in numbers too low to detect on a routine smear. That’s why a normal peripheral blood smear doesn’t exclude leukemia—bone marrow evaluation remains essential.

Other initial clues may be helpful, such as dysgranulopoiesis in the case of AML with myelodysplasia-related changes and a clinical history of cytotoxic therapy in the case of therapy-related myeloid neoplasms.

Dysgranulopoiesis refers to abnormal development of granulocytes (a type of white blood cell), seen as bizarre-looking neutrophils with irregular nuclei or abnormal granules. This is a red flag for underlying myelodysplasia, suggesting the leukemia evolved from a pre-existing bone marrow disorder. Similarly, a history of prior chemotherapy (e.g., for lymphoma or breast cancer) raises suspicion for therapy-related AML, which has distinct genetic features and a worse prognosis.

This comprehensive approach is the gold standard. The aspirate lets us examine cell morphology and perform flow cytometry (immunophenotyping), while the biopsy shows the overall architecture and extent of marrow involvement. Cytogenetics (chromosome analysis) and molecular studies (like PCR or next-generation sequencing) detect specific mutations (e.g., FLT3, NPM1, CEBPA) that refine diagnosis, predict response to therapy, and guide targeted treatment options. All these pieces fit together like a puzzle to give a complete picture of the disease.
Similarly, other hematopoietic neoplasms, such as the spectrum of MDSs, can present with pancytopenia, and many of these syndromes are defined, at least in part, by their cytopenias.

MDS, or myelodysplastic syndromes, are a group of disorders where the bone marrow produces blood cells that are dysfunctional and often destroyed before they can enter the bloodstream. Think of it as a factory with broken quality control: cells are made, but they’re misshapen and don’t work properly.
Primarily a disease of adults, MDS is commonly characterized by progressive bone marrow failure, with several of
the subtypes often progressing to AML.
This progression happens because accumulating genetic mutations push the dysplastic cells toward full-blown leukemia. It’s like a slow burn turning into a fire.

Interestingly, the mechanism of pancytopenia in hairy cell leukemia is most likely multifactorial, resulting from leukemic replacement of marrow, reticulin fibrosis, and splenomegaly with hypersplenism. Let’s unpack this: the leukemic cells physically occupy space in the marrow, leaving less room for normal hematopoiesis. They also stimulate the deposition of reticulin fibers (a type of connective tissue), which further disrupts the marrow architecture. And because the spleen often becomes enlarged, it traps blood cells and destroys them—a condition called hypersplenism. So it’s a triple hit: invasion, scarring, and splenic sequestration.

LGL can also present with a clinical picture similar to that of acquired AA. In one institution's series of patients with T-LGL, 4% of patients had AA. $^{100}$ Large granular lymphocytic (LGL) leukemia is a clonal expansion of cytotoxic T cells or natural killer (NK) cells. When it presents with pancytopenia, it can look just like aplastic anemia—low counts across the board, hypocellular marrow. So how do you tell them apart?

It is postulated that the etiology of this pancytopenia is the expansion of cytotoxic T cells, which then directly suppress hematopoiesis through direct cellular cytotoxicity or the production of cytokines. Imagine these rogue T cells as overzealous security guards that start attacking the factory workers (hematopoietic stem cells) instead of protecting them. They can kill stem cells directly or release inflammatory signals (like interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor) that shut down blood cell production. This immune-mediated suppression mimics the stem cell failure seen in AA.

In these patients, peripheral blood and bone marrow findings are similar to those of acquired AA; however, there may be a relative or absolute increase in large granular lymphocytes in the blood and/or an increased interstitial infiltrate of CD3+, CD8+, granzyme B+ lymphocytes in clusters in the bone marrow biopsy specimen $\square$ Image 11 $\square$ . $^{101}$ Granzyme B is a protein used by cytotoxic cells to kill their targets, so its presence confirms the cells are active killers. Fibrotic Diseases  
Diseases that cause fibrosis of the bone marrow can also lead to pancytopenia, most likely because of both ineffective hematopoiesis and subsequent splenomegaly with hypersplenism. Fibrosis is like scar tissue forming in the marrow—it disrupts the delicate environment where blood cells are born. The differential diagnosis of bone marrow fibrosis is extensive and includes primary myeloid neoplasms, malignant lymphomas, metastatic carcinomas, inflammatory reactions, granulomatous reactions, and osteopathies.

Many myeloid neoplasms can lead to myelofibrosis, but perhaps the myeloid neoplasms most commonly associated with bone marrow fibrosis are the myeloproliferative neoplasms. Among these neoplasms, primary myelofibrosis most often presents with bone marrow fibrosis and cytopenias. $^{107,108}$ This is a paradox: even though it’s a “proliferative” disorder, patients often have low blood counts. Why? Because the fibrosis destroys the marrow’s ability to produce blood cells effectively.

In the fibrotic stage of this disease, patients generally have anemia, and often thrombocytopenia, because of splenomegaly. However, the WBC count can be variable. $^{109}$ As fibrosis becomes more severe, the patient's cytopenias worsen. $^{110}$ The spleen often enlarges dramatically as it tries to compensate for the failing marrow—a process called extramedullary hematopoiesis. But this leads to hypersplenism, where the spleen traps and destroys blood cells, making cytopenias worse.

At diagnosis, the blood smear is often leukoerythroblastic with marked poikilocytosis, including teardrop-shaped RBCs, nucleated RBCs, giant platelets, and left-shifted myeloid cells. “Leukoerythroblastic” means that immature white and red blood cells are spilling into the bloodstream—this happens when the marrow is so scarred that cells can’t mature properly and are released early. Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) are a classic finding, caused by cells squeezing through fibrotic marrow. Giant platelets are another clue—they’re large because megakaryocytes (platelet-producing cells) are trying to compensate.

The bone marrow biopsy in this fibrotic phase demonstrates decreased cellularity, megakaryocytic atypia and clustering, and reticulin/collagen fibrosis $\square$ Image 12 $\square$ . Megakaryocytes in myelofibrosis are often bizarre—large, clustered, and with hyperlobulated nuclei. This abnormal clustering stimulates fibroblasts to produce excess reticulin and collagen, leading to fibrosis. Additional diagnostic criteria that are helpful for a diagnosis include demonstration of a $JAK2$ V617F mutation (seen in approximately 50% of patients) and an increase in serum lactate dehydrogenase levels. The $JAK2$ mutation drives uncontrolled cell signaling, contributing to the disease process. LDH is a marker of cell turnover and tissue damage, often elevated in myelofibrosis.

Of the malignant lymphomas, Hodgkin lymphoma involving the marrow is usually associated with fibrosis. In the modern era, bone marrow involvement is uncommon in Hodgkin lymphoma; in a study of 174 patients with Hodgkin disease, only 19 had bone marrow involvement at the time of presentation. $^{[111]}$ However, when the bone marrow is involved, patients can have marrow fibrosis and pancytopenia, and, in the absence of Reed-Sternberg cells, diagnosis can be challenging. $^{[112]}$ Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, but they can be sparse and hard to find. Fibrosis may be the only clue.

Interestingly, the degree of cytopenias does not appear correlated with the extent of marrow fibrosis, suggesting a possible additional mechanism of bone marrow suppression in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma. $^{[111]}$ This implies that factors beyond physical scarring—perhaps cytokines or immune-mediated suppression—are at play. Moreover, patients with an acute clinical form of Hodgkin lymphoma often present with fibrosis and pancytopenia. In a study of 9

patients with such a clinical presentation, 7 had pancytopenia, and the majority of cases involved the spleen, bone marrow, and liver. Marrow fibrosis was present in 5 patients, and the noninvolved areas of the bone marrow biopsy were either hypocellular or hypercellular.$^{113}$ What does this mean? Let’s unpack it. "Hypocellular" means there are fewer blood-forming cells than normal in those regions, suggesting suppressed blood production. "Hypercellular" means the opposite—there are more cells than expected, which might seem like a good thing, but in this context, it can reflect disordered or ineffective blood cell production. So even in areas not directly scarred by fibrosis, the bone marrow isn’t functioning properly. This tells us that the disease is having a widespread effect, not just localized damage.

Similarly, in an additional study of patients with Hodgkin lymphoma and a rapid clinical course, patients presented with fever, pancytopenia, liver dysfunction, and extensive infradiaphragmatic disease and bone marrow involvement.$^{114}$ Let’s pause and think: Why would a lymphoma cause pancytopenia? Lymphoma cells can physically invade the bone marrow, crowding out the normal stem cells that give rise to red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. When the marrow space is taken over by cancerous lymphocytes, there’s simply no room for healthy hematopoiesis—the process of making blood. The “infradiaphragmatic” involvement means disease below the diaphragm—so lymph nodes in the abdomen, spleen, liver—which aligns with the pattern of organ involvement we’ve seen. The combination of fever, multi-organ involvement, and rapid blood count decline suggests a highly aggressive disease process.

Metastatic carcinoma can also lead to bone marrow involvement and subsequent marrow fibrosis, but this occurs in fewer than 10% of patients with metastatic carcinoma and is most common in patients with lung, breast, or prostate carcinoma.$^{115–117}$ Think of it like this: cancer cells from a primary tumor—say, in the lung—can break off, travel through the bloodstream, and set up shop in the bone marrow. Once there, they grow and trigger a reactive process in the surrounding tissue. The body tries to wall off the invaders, laying down fibrous scar tissue—this is the fibrosis. Over time, this scar tissue disrupts the delicate architecture of the marrow, making it harder for blood cells to develop properly. It’s like trying to run a factory in a building that’s being slowly filled with concrete—eventually, there’s no space left for workers or machinery.

As in primary myelofibrosis, the mechanism of bone marrow failure is believed to occur because of replacement of hematopoietic tissue by abnormal tissue, with hypersplenism resulting from extramedullary hematopoiesis. Let’s break this down. “Hematopoietic tissue” is the blood-making machinery of the body, normally housed in the bone marrow. When it’s replaced—by cancer, fibrosis, or granulomas—blood cell production falters. But the body doesn’t just give up. It tries to compensate by making blood cells elsewhere—this is “extramedullary hematopoiesis,” meaning blood cell production outside the marrow (often in the spleen or liver). The spleen, now working overtime, becomes enlarged (splenomegaly), and starts trapping and destroying blood cells too aggressively—a condition called “hypersplenism.” So patients lose blood cells both because they’re not being made properly and because they’re being destroyed too quickly. It’s a double hit.

Diagnosis is usually straightforward with appropriate immunohistochemical studies and sufficient clinical history. Immunohistochemistry is like using molecular flashlights: special stains that highlight specific proteins on cells, helping us distinguish between, say, metastatic carcinoma and lymphoma. Combined with a good patient story—symptoms, timeline, lab results—the diagnosis often becomes clear.

Autoimmune fibrosis is an additional cause of fibrosis-mediated cytopenias, including pancytopenia. SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) can certainly present with pancytopenia and bone marrow fibrosis, but noncharacterized autoimmune diseases with positive autoimmune serology can also lead to modest reticulin fibrosis. Here’s a key point: not all fibrosis is cancer. Sometimes, the body’s own immune system attacks the bone marrow, causing inflammation and scarring. “Reticulin fibrosis” refers to the deposition of a delicate network of fibers (made of type III collagen) in the marrow—visible under the microscope with special silver stains. In autoimmune conditions, this fibrosis is usually mild (“modest”) compared to primary myelofibrosis.

Autoimmune fibrosis can be difficult to distinguish from primary myelofibrosis, but peripheral blood smears often lack teardrop poikilocytosis, and bone marrow biopsy generally demonstrates reactive lymphoid infiltrates in the absence of megakaryocytic clustering. Splenomegaly is also usually absent.$^{118,119}$ This is a crucial diagnostic distinction. “Teardrop poikilocytosis” refers to red blood cells that look like teardrops—this is a classic sign of primary myelofibrosis, caused by cells getting distorted as they squeeze through scarred marrow. If you don’t see teardrop cells, that’s a clue it might not be myelofibrosis. Also, in autoimmune cases, the bone marrow often shows clusters of lymphocytes that look reactive—like they’re responding to inflammation—rather than the abnormal, clustered megakaryocytes (platelet-producing cells) seen in myelofibrosis. And without significant extramedullary hematopoiesis, the spleen doesn’t enlarge. So no splenomegaly? Think autoimmune.

Granulomatous disease can also lead to pancytopenia. In a study of 38 adults with disseminated miliary tuberculosis, 3 patients presented with pancytopenia, and all 3 demonstrated granulomata in their bone marrow.$^{120}$ Granulomas are organized collections of immune cells—mainly macrophages—that form when the body tries to wall off stubborn infections like TB. When these granulomas spread throughout the marrow, they physically disrupt blood cell production. It’s like having multiple roadblocks in a highway system—traffic (blood cell development) grinds to a halt.

The mechanism of pancytopenia in such patients is unclear, but could be multifactorial, including hypersplenism, increased histiocytic phagocytosis, and bone marrow infiltration by tubercular granulomas.$^{121}$ Let’s explore each possibility. Hypersplenism, as before, means the spleen is overactive and destroys blood cells. “Histiocytic phagocytosis” refers to immune cells (histiocytes, a type of macrophage) eating up blood cells—like overzealous garbage collectors removing not just waste, but useful items too. And infiltration by granulomas directly destroys marrow architecture. So again, multiple mechanisms can gang up to cause low blood counts.

Osteopathies can also lead to bone marrow fibrosis and subsequent pancytopenia. Vitamin D–dependent rickets in breastfed infants has been reported to lead to marrow fibrosis and pancytopenia, most likely because of secondary hyperparathyroidism, which can cause osteosclerosis.$^{122}$ This is a fascinating connection. Rickets is a disease of weak, soft bones due to vitamin D deficiency. In response, the body increases parathyroid hormone (PTH) to try to fix calcium levels—this is “secondary hyperparathyroidism.” High PTH leads to increased bone turnover and, in some cases, abnormal bone hardening (osteosclerosis). As bone structure changes, the marrow space gets compressed and replaced with fibrous tissue. Less space for marrow means fewer blood cells—hence pancytopenia.

Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and patients with renal osteodystrophy receiving long-term dialysis have also been known to develop bone marrow fibrosis, osteomalacia, increased osteoclastic activity, and splenomegaly, with resulting pancytopenia $\square$ Image 13 $\square$.$^{123}$ Renal osteodystrophy is a bone disease that occurs in people with chronic kidney failure. Their kidneys can’t activate vitamin D or excrete phosphate, leading to mineral imbalances. This triggers high PTH, bone breakdown, and abnormal bone remodeling. Over time, this disrupts the marrow environment. “Osteomalacia” means soft bones (the adult version of rickets), and “increased osteoclastic activity” means bone is being broken down too aggressively. All of this contributes to a hostile environment for blood cell production. And again, splenomegaly can develop due to extramedullary hematopoiesis—trying to compensate for failed marrow function.

Additional laboratory

studies, such as serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels, can be helpful in this setting. For example, abnormally high calcium levels might raise suspicion for certain malignancies like multiple myeloma or lymphoma, which can infiltrate the bone marrow and disrupt blood cell production. Similarly, parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels help distinguish between primary hyperparathyroidism and other causes of hypercalcemia, which is important because some tumors can cause high calcium through different mechanisms (like producing a PTH-related protein). So, while these tests don’t directly measure blood cell production, they provide indirect clues about systemic conditions that could be driving the pancytopenia.

To summarize, the causes of new-onset pancytopenia are vast and extremely varied. Think of the bone marrow as a factory that produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Pancytopenia means all three types of blood cells are low—so something is disrupting the entire production line. The problem could be inside the factory itself (like a failure of stem cells or bone marrow infiltration), or it could be due to external factors (like toxins, autoimmune destruction, or nutritional deficiencies). Because so many different problems can lead to the same end result, pinpointing the exact cause is like solving a complex puzzle.

Here we have provided a general overview of some of the more common causes of pancytopenia in both children and adults; however, this list is by no means complete, and patients with complex conditions may have multifactorial causes of pancytopenia. For instance, a patient might have both a nutritional deficiency *and* an underlying autoimmune disorder contributing to low blood counts. In such cases, treating only one factor may not fully resolve the pancytopenia, which is why a comprehensive evaluation is essential.

The diagnosis, especially in the absence of obvious neoplasm, can be extraordinarily challenging even in the presence of sharp clinical acumen; therefore, numerous studies, including peripheral smear examination and bone marrow biopsy, are often required to make an accurate diagnosis. The peripheral smear is like a snapshot of what circulating blood cells look like—do they appear normal, or are there abnormal shapes, sizes, or fragments that hint at a deeper problem? A bone marrow biopsy, on the other hand, is like going straight to the factory floor: it allows us to see how active the marrow is, whether it’s packed with abnormal cells (like leukemia or metastatic cancer), or whether it’s empty (as in aplastic anemia). These tools, combined with clinical history, physical findings, and targeted lab tests, help build a complete picture.
